faqs.question: How do you write "I love you" in Punjabi?
faqs.answer: A man writes ਮੈਂ ਤੈਨੂੰ ਪਿਆਰ ਕਰਦਾ ਹਾਂ (maĩ tainū̃ piār kardā hā̃); a woman writes ਮੈਂ ਤੈਨੂੰ ਪਿਆਰ ਕਰਦੀ ਹਾਂ (maĩ tainū̃ piār kardī hā̃). The only difference is the verb ending, which agrees with the writer's gender rather than the reader's.

faqs.question: Should I write my love letter in Gurmukhi or Roman Punjabi?
faqs.answer: Gurmukhi if she reads it, Roman if she only speaks the language. faqs.question: Is it ਤੂੰ or ਤੁਸੀਂ for a girlfriend?

faqs.question: Does the Punjabi verb change if I am a woman writing to my girlfriend?

faqs.question: What is the difference between Gurmukhi and Shahmukhi?
faqs.answer: They are two unrelated scripts for the same language. Gurmukhi, a modified Landa script, is used in Indian Punjab; Shahmukhi is a Perso-Arabic variant used in Pakistani Punjab, where Carmen Brandt's 2014 chapter records around 60 million Punjabi speakers. They share no letters, so a letter in one is unreadable to someone who only knows the other.

A short letter she can hear in your voice lands better than a long one that reads as translated.

faqs.question: What should I call her in a Punjabi love letter?
faqs.answer: ਪਿਆਰੀ (piārī, "dear") is the neutral opening. ਨੀ (nī) is the vocative particle used to address a female, as in the folk line ਮਾਏ ਨੀ ਮਾਏ, and it is warm but village-inflected. ਹੀਰ (hīr) works as a common noun for a beloved woman as well as the name from the Heer Ranjha qissa.

faqs.question: Why is ਹੈਂ romanised as "aĩ" and not "hain"?
faqs.answer: Because the initial ਹ in that copula is a tone marker rather than a pronounced /h/, which is why the Punjabi University dictionary writes ਹੈਂ as aĩ and ਹੋ as o. Romanisations that keep the h are the main reason so many transliterated Punjabi lines online sound wrong when read out.

# Love Letter for Girlfriend in Punjabi, in Gurmukhi and Roman

A love letter for girlfriend in Punjabi turns on four decisions rather than on finding better words: which script she reads, whether you call her ਤੂੰ or ਤੁਸੀਂ, whether the verb carries your gender or hers, and where the letter lands. The "I love you" page is the most-created template on SubhSandesh — 987 pages, 29.2% of everything made since 2026-03-12 — and the most-viewed, at 14,607 views, 35.2% of all 41,486 page views recorded to 2026-09-02. Half of those views, 50.3%, happen on a phone.

That last figure settles more than the wording does: a phone holds Gurmukhi and a romanisation on one screen, where paper cannot. What follows is the script choice, the pronoun choice, four short letters with a line-by-line romanisation, and the two grammar errors running through most Punjabi samples online.

## The four decisions a Punjabi love letter forces

Punjabi makes you commit to things English lets you leave vague. Before the first sentence you have chosen a script, a level of intimacy, a gender for your own verb, and a vocative.

Get the pronoun wrong and a letter meant to sound close reads like a bank form. Get the verb gender wrong and it reads as though somebody else wrote it — which, on most sample pages, somebody did.

One note on the romanisation below. I write the pronounced form, so ਪਿਆਰ is *piār*, not the *piāra* dictionary convention prints with its inherent final vowel, and I mark the silent tonal ਹ: the Punjabi University dictionary romanises ਹੈਂ as *aĩ* and ਹੋ as *o*, because that initial ਹ is a tone marker rather than a pronounced /h/. It is why so many romanised Punjabi lines online sound wrong read aloud.

## Gurmukhi, Shahmukhi or Roman: which script she reads

Punjabi is written three ways, and which she reads depends on where her family is from. Carmen Brandt's 2014 chapter in *Language Endangerment and Preservation in South Asia* records around 60 million Punjabi speakers in Pakistan — 44.15% of the population on the 1998 census — writing it in a Perso-Arabic variant called Shahmukhi, "from the Shah's mouth". In India it is the first language of barely 30 million people on the 2001 census, who mostly write [Gurmukhi](https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/items/3591e3b1-c7a8-46c5-9fca-46f88cbf6443), a modified Landa script used for almost nothing else.

Gurmukhi is the safe default for a girlfriend in Indian Punjab or the Sikh diaspora; Shahmukhi is the one to ask about if her family is from Pakistani Punjab. Do not guess between them — they share no letters.

Roman Punjabi is the third option, and the honest one if she speaks Punjabi but never learned to read it. Mukul Saxena's 1995 York doctoral study of 86 Panjabi Hindu informants in Southall, surveyed across 1988–89, found that when they wrote a personal letter to a South Asian friend in the UK, [only 7.4% wrote it in Punjabi](http://etheses.whiterose.ac.uk/21070/1/712124.pdf) against 63.0% in English; to relatives in India the Punjabi share rose to 21.0%. A love letter for gf in Punjabi she cannot decode is a gift she has to work at.

## ਤੂੰ or ਤੁਸੀਂ: the pronoun that sets the tone

ਤੂੰ (*tū̃*) is the intimate singular; ਤੁਸੀਂ (*tusī̃*) is the plural and the respectful form. To a girlfriend, use ਤੂੰ — that is the choice in every letter below, and it is deliberate. ਤੁਸੀਂ to a partner reads either as distance or, in a family where it is the normal spousal address, as a slightly formal joke.

The dative forms differ too, which is where sample letters come apart: ਤੂੰ takes ਤੈਨੂੰ (*tainū̃*, "to you"), ਤੁਸੀਂ takes ਤੁਹਾਨੂੰ (*tuhānū̃*). So do the copulas — ਤੂੰ ... ਹੈਂ (*aĩ*) against ਤੁਸੀਂ ... ਹੋ (*o*).

The intimate form carries extra weight in Punjabi specifically. Suraiya Alam's 2011 study in the *International Journal of Linguistics*, working with Punjabi-Pakistani speakers in London, found [Punjabi serving the "tu" relationships and Urdu the "vous" ones](https://macrothink.org/journal/index.php/ijl/article/download/944/922) — the language itself was the intimacy marker, and switching out of it out-grouped the listener. Writing to her in Punjabi at all is already half the message.

## Four short love letters in Punjabi, with romanisation

Each is short on purpose. A short love letter for girlfriend in Punjabi that is correct beats six long ones that are not, and short is what a phone screen holds without scrolling. Every line uses dictionary-verified words; the forms I could not verify are named in this post's audit rather than hidden.

### 1. The plain one, written by a man

ਪਿਆਰੀ [her name],
ਮੈਂ ਤੈਨੂੰ ਪਿਆਰ ਕਰਦਾ ਹਾਂ।
ਤੂੰ ਮੇਰੀ ਜਾਨ ਹੈਂ।
ਤੇਰੇ ਬਿਨਾਂ ਦਿਲ ਨਹੀਂ ਲੱਗਦਾ।
ਤੇਰਾ, [your name]

*piārī [her name], / maĩ tainū̃ piār kardā hā̃. / tū̃ merī jān aĩ. / tere binā̃ dil nahī̃ laggdā. / terā, [your name]*

"Dear ___, I love you. You are my life. Without you nothing settles." Note ਕਰਦਾ — masculine, because it agrees with the writer.

### 2. The same letter, written by a woman

ਪਿਆਰੀ [her name],
ਮੈਂ ਤੈਨੂੰ ਪਿਆਰ ਕਰਦੀ ਹਾਂ।
ਤੂੰ ਮੇਰੀ ਜਾਨ ਹੈਂ।
ਮੈਂ ਹਮੇਸ਼ਾ ਤੇਰੇ ਨਾਲ ਹਾਂ।
ਤੇਰੀ, [your name]

*piārī [her name], / maĩ tainū̃ piār kardī hā̃. / tū̃ merī jān aĩ. / maĩ hameśā tere nāl hā̃. / terī, [your name]*

One character changes and the whole letter changes hands: ਕਰਦਾ becomes ਕਰਦੀ, ਤੇਰਾ becomes ਤੇਰੀ. Punjabi's habitual verb agrees with the speaker's gender, so a man cannot copy a woman's letter and a woman cannot copy a man's.

### 3. The folk-song register

ਨੀ ਸੋਹਣੀ,
ਮੈਂ ਤੈਨੂੰ ਹਮੇਸ਼ਾ ਪਿਆਰ ਕਰਦਾ ਹਾਂ।
ਤੂੰ ਮੇਰੀ ਸੋਹਣੀ ਹੀਰ ਹੈਂ।

*nī sohṇī, / maĩ tainū̃ hameśā piār kardā hā̃. / tū̃ merī sohṇī hīr aĩ.*

ਹੀਰ (*hīr*) is Heer of the Heer Ranjha qissa, and the Punjabi University dictionary lists it as a common noun for a beloved woman too; ਰਾਂਝਾ (*rāñjhā*) does that job for a man.

ਨੀ (*nī*) is the vocative for a female addressee — the particle in the folk line ਮਾਏ ਨੀ ਮਾਏ. Its counterpart ਵੇ (*ve*) is what women use to men. It is warm and village-inflected, which is either exactly right or exactly wrong depending on how you two talk.

### 4. The respectful version, for early days or a letter her family may see

ਪਿਆਰੀ [her name],
ਮੈਂ ਤੁਹਾਨੂੰ ਪਿਆਰ ਕਰਦਾ ਹਾਂ।
ਤੁਸੀਂ ਮੇਰੀ ਜਾਨ ਹੋ।

*piārī [her name], / maĩ tuhānū̃ piār kardā hā̃. / tusī̃ merī jān o.*

Use this one sparingly — it is the version for a letter that will be read aloud with her parents in the room.

## The two mistakes in most Punjabi love letter text online

The first is the copula. With ਤੂੰ, the verb "to be" is ਹੈਂ (*aĩ*), not ਹੈ (*hai*). Many of the Punjabi sample letters circulating for this query pair ਤੂੰ with third-person ਹੈ, which reads as nonstandard even where speech is loose about it.

The second is romanisation, or its absence. The two largest Punjabi sample-letter pages ranking for this query carried 4,618 and 5,580 Gurmukhi characters between them when I measured them on 2026-09-02, and not one line of romanisation. Against Saxena's 7.4%, that is a page built for the minority of Punjabi speakers who read the script.

Third, softer: the letter has to survive being sent. A shared [romantic "I love you" page with the letter typed onto the cover](https://subhsandesh.in/love-gf) keeps Gurmukhi and romanisation fixed on one screen instead of scrolling apart. The median gap between first save and last edit on that template is 7.2 hours across all 987 of them — not the behaviour of people firing off a message.

## Script, romanisation and reach compared

What differs between the ways of delivering the same four lines.

| Option | Script she must decode | Both scripts visible at once | First-party data to 2026-09-02 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Handwritten on paper | Gurmukhi or Shahmukhi only | Only if you hand-write two lines | No view data — paper is unmeasurable |
| WhatsApp message | Gurmukhi or Roman | Yes, but the thread scrolls past it | No first-party data |
| "I love you" page (/love-gf) | Either, side by side | Yes, fixed on the cover | 987 created, 14,607 views, 50.3% on a phone |
| [Darling page](https://subhsandesh.in/darling) (/darling) | Either, side by side | Yes | 349 created, 10.3% of all pages |

Paper wins on sentiment and loses on romanisation; a page is the only row where both scripts stay put.

## When a Punjabi love letter is the wrong choice

If she does not read Gurmukhi and would be embarrassed to admit it, a Punjabi letter is a test disguised as a gift. Send it in Roman, or say the line out loud instead.

If Punjabi is a language she has actively moved away from, be careful. Sham Haidar and colleagues, interviewing 60 Punjabi students aged 18–22 at four universities in Islamabad in 2019, found speakers [disowning the language and the identity with it](https://revije.ff.uni-lj.si/ala/article/view/9449) — one was mocked by friends for speaking Punjabi on the phone, and women in the sample were least likely to use it or pass it on. That is Pakistani Punjab and Indian Punjab differs, but the risk holds anywhere: a language can carry shame as easily as warmth.

A page is the wrong container twice over. If she has no smartphone, the 50.3% phone figure is against you. If the surprise depends on nobody else seeing it, 42.8% of creators password-protect before sharing — 1,444 of 3,377 pages — a step you must remember.

One argument for Punjabi over English anyway. Jean-Marc Dewaele's 2011 review reports that in Aneta Pavlenko's analysis of 1,039 multilinguals, [65% said they feel like a different person when they change language](https://eprints.bbk.ac.uk/id/eprint/5096/1/Dewaele2011Anglistik.pdf), and cites a study where the same story in Greek drew sympathy from Greek-English bilinguals while the English version drew indifference.

If Punjabi is the language you argue and joke in, it is the language the sentence lands in. Browse the [full set of shareable templates](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) if the letter needs a photo or a song behind it.

auditReport.honestAssessment:
It is the only page for this query that pairs every Gurmukhi line with a romanisation and names the four decisions a Punjabi letter forces — script (Gurmukhi vs Shahmukhi vs Roman), ਤੂੰ vs ਤੁਸੀਂ, the writer's-gender verb form (ਕਰਦਾ/ਕਰਦੀ) and the ਨੀ vocative. The two sample pages ranking above it carried 4,618 and 5,580 Gurmukhi characters and zero romanised lines when measured on 2026-09-02, and no page in the top ten cites a single dated source. That plus Saxena's 7.4% letter-writing figure and SubhSandesh's own 987-page / 14,607-view / 50.3%-phone data is the citable material. Domain authority is far below Pinterest, Instagram and Wikipedia, all of which currently rank on this query, so expect months and no promise of a position.

LANGUAGE FLAGS FOR NATIVE REVIEW — I am not a native Punjabi speaker. Every word printed was checked against its English Wiktionary Punjabi entry on 2026-09-02, but the following composed forms and judgements were NOT verifiable and need a native reader before this is trusted:
1. ਪਿਆਰੀ (piārī) as the letter opening in letters 1, 2 and 4 — inferred as the feminine of ਪਿਆਰਾ (piārā, verified "dear, beloved"); ਪਿਆਰੀ itself has no Wiktionary Punjabi entry.
2. ਲੱਗਦਾ (laggdā) in "ਤੇਰੇ ਬਿਨਾਂ ਦਿਲ ਨਹੀਂ ਲੱਗਦਾ" (letter 1) — ਲੱਗਣਾ (laggaṇā) is verified but the inflected habitual participle is not, and the whole phrase is an idiom I could not verify as a fixed expression. If it is wrong, drop that line.
3. "ਦਿਲ ਨਹੀਂ ਲੱਗਦਾ" glossed as "nothing settles" — my gloss, not a dictionary gloss.
4. ਤੂੰ ਮੇਰੀ ਜਾਨ ਹੈਂ (letters 1, 2) — ਜਾਨ is verified as "life, soul" but its gender is not stated in the entry I read; ਮੇਰੀ assumes it is feminine.
5. ਮੈਂ ਹਮੇਸ਼ਾ ਤੇਰੇ ਨਾਲ ਹਾਂ (letter 2) — every word verified, the word order and the oblique ਤੇਰੇ before the postposition ਨਾਲ are my construction.
6. ਤੂੰ ਮੇਰੀ ਸੋਹਣੀ ਹੀਰ ਹੈਂ (letter 3) — ਹੀਰ is verified as a common noun for a beloved woman, but using it with the attributive ਸੋਹਣੀ in a written letter may read as pastiche.
7. Whether ਨੀ is acceptable to a girlfriend at all. The dictionary attests it as a vocative to a female ("ਮਾਏ ਨੀ ਮਾਏ") and it is common in song, but the register may read as rustic or presumptuous in a written letter. I said so in the body; a native reader should confirm or kill letter 3.
8. Letter 4's ਤੁਸੀਂ register: ਮੈਂ ਤੁਹਾਨੂੰ ਪਿਆਰ ਕਰਦਾ ਹਾਂ and ਤੁਸੀਂ ਮੇਰੀ ਜਾਨ ਹੋ. Both ਤੁਹਾਨੂੰ and ਹੋ are verified individually; the sentences are composed, and whether ਤੁਸੀਂ to a girlfriend reads as respectful or as parody is exactly the judgement I cannot make.
9. ਸੋਹਣੀਏ (sohṇīe), the song-register vocative, has no Wiktionary entry and is therefore NOT printed anywhere in the post even though it is the form readers will have heard. Worth adding if a native reader confirms it.
10. My claim that pairing ਤੂੰ with third-person ਹੈ "reads as nonstandard" is my own reading of the circulating samples, not a sourced grammatical judgement. Colloquial Punjabi may be looser than I allow.
11. Romanisation scheme: I write the pronounced form (ਪਿਆਰ as piār) where Wiktionary writes the inherent-vowel form (piāra), and I follow the dictionary's silent-tonal-ਹ convention (ਹੈਂ = aĩ, ਹੋ = o) while writing ਹਾਂ as hā̃ rather than ā̃. That last inconsistency is deliberate for readability but it is an inconsistency, and a reviewer may prefer one scheme throughout.

OTHER GAPS. The Pricing block in facts.md is empty, so the post says nothing about cost in any direction — but a reader on this query plausibly wants to know whether making a shareable page costs anything, and neither the body nor an FAQ answers it. That is a real content hole, not an oversight; fill the manual pricing block in facts.md and it becomes a thirteenth FAQ. Separately, Saxena's letter-writing figures are from a 1988-89 survey of Panjabi Hindus specifically, a community that leans toward Devanagari, so the 7.4% almost certainly understates Gurmukhi letter-writing among Sikh families; the post states the community and the survey dates but a newer Indian-Punjab equivalent would be a better number and I could not find one that was open-access.
